candidates.source_summary: Two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a man died in hospital following a fall from a balcony at an address on Liverpool Street, Salford.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
A man initially arrested on suspicion of attempted murder has now been arrested on suspicion of murder. A second man has also been arrested on suspicion of murder.

Officers were called shortly after midnight on Saturday morning, 29th August, to reports that a man had fallen from a balcony at an address on Liverpool Street.

Emergency services attended, and the man was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries. He died in hospital on the evening of Saturday, 29th August.

Both men remain in police custody for questioning.

A Home Office post-mortem examination is due to take place today.

Chief Inspector Lee Gridley from GMP’s Salford district said: “Firstly, our thoughts remain with the man’s family and friends as they grieve the death of their loved one.

“We now have two men in custody, and they are being questioned by detectives.

“The investigation is progressing at pace, and we have a team of detectives working to establish the full circumstances that led to this tragic incident.

“We understand that incidents of this nature may cause concern within the community; however, we believe this is an isolated incident and that there is no wider risk to the public.

“We would like to hear from anyone who may have information that can assist us. Anyone that was in the Liverpool Street area of Salford around the time of this incident, or who has mobile phone, CCTV, Ring doorbell and dashcam footage, can contact police on 101 and quote log 8 of 29/08/2026. Reports can also be made via the LiveChat function at gmp.police.uk

“Alternatively contact the independent charity Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.”

The matter has been referred to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) due to the parties having earlier contact with the police, as is standard with incidents of this nature.

candidates.source_summary: Young adult care-leavers have a death rate about four times higher than the general population.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Hayden said he would like to see significant changes in the care system A teenager who went into care when he was 10 has described how he struggled to navigate the system and seek help. Hayden, now aged 17, lived in a children's home until he was 16 before moving into a semi-independent home. After feeling unsafe there he ended up sofa-surfing. "There is an incredible amount of individuals working so hard to improve the lives of young people but the system is fundamentally flawed," said Hayden, who got in touch with the BBC via Your Voice to share his experience. A new government-commissioned report found that young adult care-leavers have a death rate about four times higher than the general population . The report noted the potentially catastrophic consequences for those who are often left alone "with no safety net". People leaving care in England at 18 often lose "significant levers of support", the report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed. "You kind of are navigating it by yourself and just hoping you've said the right things and put the right things forward to make things happen," said Hayden, who grew up in Middleton, Greater Manchester, before being placed in care in a different local authority area.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Cyber crime takes many forms and can have a devastating impact on victims. Some may lose money while others may fall victim to identity theft and have to deal with the consequences of criminals racking up huge debts in their name. To help people deal with the risks of life online, Greater Manchester Police’s Economic and Cyber Crime Unit is holding a series of drop-in events across the borough. GMP shared: “With the internet at the centre of daily life, it’s inevitable that there are many kinds of fraud to go along with it. This can be anything from identity theft, online transactions, dating scams and more, all designed to fool you and take your money. “With scams ranging from the simplest confidence trick to the most sophisticated high-tech online fraud, it pays to keep up to date with the latest news and advice. “Several million cases of fraud and of computer misuse are reported to the police every year. It’s staggering, but even more staggering is that so many of those crimes could have been prevented by making a few small changes in online behaviour. “To avoid becoming a victim of online crime you don’t need to be a computer expert. Developing a few good online habits drastically reduces your chances of becoming a victim of cyber crime, makes you less vulnerable and lets you use the web safely.” Steps you can take to reduce the risk of cybercrime include never sharing passwords or personal details and make sure passwords cannot easily be guessed.

candidates.source_summary: Jaden Williams scores a late winner off the bench as Colchester beat winless Rochdale in League Two.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Jaden Williams came off the bench to score a late winner as Colchester beat winless Rochdale at the JobServe Community Stadium. Williams brilliantly steered a first-time effort into the top corner from Kane Vincent-Young's cross in the 87th minute to break the deadlock for the U's and secure them back-to-back wins. Colchester almost took a sixth-minute lead when Jack Payne's shot flew straight at keeper Nils Ramming, after Oscar Thorn had delivered a low cross into the six-yard box. Kane Taylor then nodded wide from Dan Moss's cross for the Dale. But the U's came close to breaking the deadlock just before the half hour as Brad Ihionvien's close-range shot deflected wide for a corner when it looked a certain goal, after Payne had done well to carve out the chance. Ryan East's deflected long-range strike flew just wide for Rochdale early in the second half while at the other end, Harry Anderson's powerful strike was palmed away by the diving Dale keeper Nils Ramming, before Williams struck. Cowley: 'To win late on is a good habit' Colchester United have won just one of their last 10 Football League games against Rochdale (D4 L5), though it came in the last match in this fixture, a 2-1 victory in January 2023.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: <h3>What you need to know as old faces return to the JCS...</h3> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h4>The Match</h4> <p>The U&rsquo;s take on Rochdale AFC at the JobServe Community Stadium on Saturday 29th August.</p> <p>Danny and Nicky&rsquo;s side head into the game on the back of their first League Two win of the season, beating Oldham Athletic 2-1 at the JobServe Community Stadium last time out. Harry Anderson&rsquo;s second-half leveller and a stoppage-time Lewis Temple own goal secured all three points. Academy striker Kien Connolly is expected to keep his place in the matchday squad following his senior debut against Oldham.</p> <p>This weekend&rsquo;s match offers the U&rsquo;s the chance to build on that result and pick up back-to-back league wins, ahead of a week of away fixtures &ndash; a trip to <a href="https://tickets.colchesterunited.net/Tickets/BuyTickets/SeatSelection/40202" target="_blank">Bristol Rovers in midweek on Tuesday 1st September</a> and a journey to <a href="https://tickets.colchesterunited.net/Tickets/BuyTickets/SeatSelection/40206" target="_blank">Swindon Town on Saturday 5<sup>th</sup> September.</a> Tickets for these away fixtures are still available to purchase until Sunday and Thursday, respectively.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h4>The Opponents</h4> <p>Rochdale AFC, known as the Dale, arrive at the JobServe Community Stadium having lost both of their opening two League Two fixtures, going down 3-0 away at Newport County before falling to a 1-2 home defeat to Crawley Town last Saturday.</p> <p>The Dale return to the Football League for the first time since their relegation to the National League at the end of the 2022/23 season, having won promotion via the play-offs with a penalty shoot-out victory over Boreham Wood at Wembley in May after finishing runners-up behind champions York City.</p> <p>Rochdale&rsquo;s route into this season&rsquo;s League Two campaign also included a Carabao Cup exit, beating Tranmere Rovers on penalties in the preliminary round before going down 2-0 away to League One side Bradford City in round one.</p> <p>Head coach Ian Watson took charge of the Dale in June, joining from National League North side South Shields, where he led the club to a second-place finish and a promotion final appearance in his first full season in charge. He replaced Jimmy McNulty, who departed for League One club Stockport County.</p> <p>Watson has overseen a significant rebuild over the summer, with new arrivals including goalkeeper Nils Ramming, centre-back Laurence Maguire, and Chelsea loanee Kaiden Wilson, alongside forwards Cian Hayes and Zain Silcott-Duberry. Saturday could also mark a return to Essex for the ever-present Ian Henderson. In a period spanning three years, the striker netted 26 goals and provided nine assists in 129 appearances for the U&rsquo;s in the early 2010s.</p> <p>The two sides have not met since the 2022/23 season, when a first-half Devante Rodney penalty gave Rochdale a 1-0 win at the JobServe Community Stadium in September 2022 before the U&rsquo;s claimed all three points in Greater Manchester in January 2023.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h4>The Matchday</h4> <p>We&rsquo;re at home in Sky Bet League Two action once again!

candidates.source_body_excerpt: By SOPHIE CHURCH - POLITICAL REPORTER 16:03 28 Aug 2026, updated 16:19 28 Aug 2026 Ed Miliband ’s efforts to deport the ringleader of the Rochdale grooming gang came to nothing this week after Pakistan refused to take him back. Mohammad Ishaq Dar, Pakistan’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister, informed Mr Miliband in a meeting on Thursday Pakistan would not accept Shabir Ahmed back because it was not legally bound to do so. Pakistani officials told their British counterparts they ‘currently do not have any legislation or formal mechanism under which we can take him back’. Ahmed, who was convicted of 30 child rape offences, was released in July this year after serving 14 years behind bars. While he has been stripped of his British citizenship, ministers are facing difficulties deporting him because Commonwealth citizens arriving in Britain before 1973 are protected from removal under archaic legislation. Pakistan has long claimed Ahmed is Britain’s responsibility as he renounced his Pakistani citizenship long ago, and has spent virtually his entire life in the UK . Mr Miliband, who Andy Burnham made Foreign Secretary on entering No 10, pressed Mr Dar to consider taking the criminal back in a meeting at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office for the pair's first meeting.

candidates.source_summary: The restoration of a unique set of historic steps which are more than 400 years old old has been completed in the heart of Rochdale town centre.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The restoration of a unique set of historic steps which are more than 400 years old old has been completed in the heart of Rochdale town centre. Running through the Broadfield Park Slopes, the Packer Spout steps link the major historic attractions of Rochdale Town Hall and its surrounding area to St Chad’s Church, the oldest church in the borough, parts of which have Saxon origins. Dating from sometime before 1660, the church steps have a rich history and were thought to be used by mourning relatives who would travel up the steps to St Chad’s Church, where they would scatter rue and rosemary in ‘God’s Acre’ (St Chad’s Churchyard) as an offering to ease the spirits of their loved ones. Situated in the recently restored Broadfield Park Slopes area, during the Victorian period, the steps ran directly through a notorious slum area, known as ‘the gank’. The gank was characterised by tightly packed housing, narrow passageways, high crime rates and large numbers of ‘houses of ill repute’. Many of the residents who worked in Rochdale’s mills would have lived out their lives in this area. The site is so steep that Oldham contractor Maysand, which delivered the work, had to devise a special pulley system with tracks and rollers to help transport the stone up the hill. READ MORE: Police target organised gang over 19 violent Parklife robberies The team had to painstakingly remove all 122 steps, many of which had become broken and uneven, before reconstructing both the area underneath and the damaged steps using traditional sandstone, to match the existing stone.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Police have arrested seven people following a spate of violent robberies at festivals in both Manchester and London. Officers from Greater Manchester Police (GMP) and the Metropolitan Police Service (Met), have carried out a series of coordinated strikes against a suspected organised crime group at addresses across London on Wednesday morning. The investigation was launched after 19 violent robberies were reported at Parklife Festival in Manchester in July this year. Victims reported being approached in crowded areas of the festival and asked to hand over valuable items, including mobile phones and jewellery. In several incidents, those who resisted, or who’s friends stepped in to help, were subjected to violence before their property was stolen. Investigators believe members of the group would walk through the crowds and pass stolen items back and forth making it difficult to track where the items had gone. Officers responded immediately to reports of the offences and carried out extensive CCTV enquiries during the festival, which led to the identification of a suspect by the victims. Following his arrest on suspicion of robbery, investigators seized and examined his mobile phone, uncovering evidence which indicated a wider criminal network in operation.

candidates.source_summary: A Wardle man who has been in recovery from substance use for just over a year has contributed to a new poetry and audio walking trail.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
A Wardle man who has been in recovery from substance use for just over a year has contributed to a new poetry and audio walking trail.

John Bailey is one of 15 people from Turning Point's Rochdale and Oldham Active Recovery service, known as ROAR, who worked with poet Phil Davenport on the project.

The group created seven spoken poetry pieces for If You Could Speak to the World, a self-guided walking route from Oldham town centre into Northern Roots.

Their recordings have been combined with music composed by Sophie Cooper and performed by Milnrow Band.

Mr Bailey, a former bar and restaurant manager, took part in outdoor sessions at Northern Roots during the spring and early summer.

The participants, aged from their 20s to their 70s, used the landscape to help create poetry and record sounds for the trail.

They also helped map the route and identify stopping points.

Mr Bailey said: “A big part of my recovery has been saying yes to things. And as an English literature graduate who grew up going on lots of walks, this opportunity really stood out for me.”

He is currently undertaking peer mentor training with ROAR ahead of postgraduate study in counselling and psychotherapy.

Describing one of the techniques used during the project, he said: “Phil had us write down answers to three questions: who we were grateful to and what message we would send them, what we look back on with sadness and what we thought the area we were walking through was like 150 years ago.

“We then 'curated' our own words to make a 'found poem' out of them. They were surprisingly profound and beautiful and, in this way, everyone in the group created a piece they could feel proud of.”

The shortest version of the trail is two miles and takes in all seven locations, while longer routes run for up to six miles.

Maps will be available from the Northern Roots Welcome Building and online from September.

Davenport said: “This is a sound walk like no other. We aren’t delivering a nature trail or a local history, but something much more unusual. We will be guided by the voices of local people in recovery: people who are intensely aware of the dark art of damage and the honesty needed to pull away from it.

“Their poems are the narrative for the walk, which takes us out of a busy, chaotic town centre, to the edge of where people are and then out beyond, into the woods and the wilds.”

The project was commissioned by visual arts organisation Portraits of Recovery for Recoverist Month and funded through Transport for Greater Manchester's Wheels and Walks programme.

Guided walks are due to take place during September and October to launch the permanent audio trail.
candidates.source_title: Wardle man lends his voice to poetry trail about recovery

candidates.source_summary: A drug dealer who was shot in the arm by police as officers attempted to arrest him in Whitefield has been jailed for six years and 10 months.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Lewis Hanson was sentenced at Manchester Crown Court today, Thursday 27 August, after admitting drug and firearms offences.

Hanson, 20, of no fixed address, pleaded guilty to possession with intent to supply Class A and B drugs, possession of a prohibited firearm, conspiracy to supply a firearm, possession of ammunition and being concerned in the supply of controlled drugs.

Greater Manchester Police's Serious and Organised Crime Group had been monitoring Hanson's movements on Friday 22 May.

Police said he was seen driving a white Cupra Ateca around Radcliffe, Whitefield and Greenmount and repeatedly returning to an address in Chapelfield.

Officers also saw Hanson meeting a number of people in what police believed was activity consistent with suspected drug supply.

At around 3pm, officers attempted to stop the Cupra on Bury New Road in Whitefield.

GMP said Hanson attempted to evade arrest and an officer discharged a single shot, striking him in the arm.

He was detained and taken to hospital. Police said his injury was not life-threatening or life-changing.

Officers subsequently searched the address in Chapelfield and recovered a converted Retay Model 17 blank-firing pistol, which is prohibited under the Firearms Act.

Ammunition was found concealed in a black bin bag inside a bedroom wardrobe.

Police also seized Class A and B drugs, scales, vacuum-packed bags and empty snap bags.

Detective Superintendent Joe Harrop, of GMP's Serious Crime Division, said: “Hanson played a key role in the supply of illegal drugs throughout Bury and beyond, our investigation uncovered evidence of drug dealing and with the recovery of a prohibited firearm at an address linked to him.

“Ammunition and drug supply paraphernalia were also found, underlining the lengths he may have gone to, to protect his interests.

“The presence of a converted firearm in these circumstances is deeply concerning and demonstrates the dangerous environment often associated with organised criminal activity.

“Drug dealing and firearms have a devastating impact on our communities. They fuel exploitation, violence and fear, and we know that residents want this type of criminality removed from their area, and we are doing all we can to do exactly that.

“We will continue to relentlessly pursue those involved in the supply of drugs, the possession of illegal firearms and organised criminality. We remain committed to protecting our communities, disrupting criminal networks and bringing offenders to justice.”

By 2027, all council employees will have the option of receiving the extra as a lump sum or in staggered amounts. The change, agreed by the council, follows a petition organised by school support workers and signed by more than 900 people. Previously, the council only paid backpay as a lump sum. That meant it was treated as additional income for Universal Credit recipients and resulted in benefit payments being reduced or stopped the following month. In some cases, student loan repayments could also be affected, says Unison. The new system will allow staff to spread backpay across Universal Credit assessment periods, helping to limit the financial blow.
